title: Every requirement raised for this system, where it came from, and whether it holds
summary:
One hundred and one requirements — functional and non-functional — mined from nine commits, the 88 gap entries on the six pages beside this one, the migrations that are the real contract, and three external findings that never touched the code. Each carries an origin, a status verified against this tree rather than copied from the commit that claimed it, and the command that decided it.

**Eighty-six rows are `met` outright**, eleven more are `met` in one dimension, three are `decided`, and **one is open**: tiers 3 and 4 against real hardware. There is no phone attached to the machine this was built on. Everything leading to `USBDEVFS_RESET` and `uhubctl` is written, tested, and has been run on Linux — discovery reads a hub's per-port switchability from the kernel's own file mode — but reading that a port can be switched is not switching it, and this register does not pretend otherwise.

Read it for three things the area pages cannot show. The couplings: one guard in `runNode` once blocked four separate requirements. The wrong remedies — a surface that tells an operator something is protected when it is not is worse than a documented absence, and this register has found five of them, the most recent being a reference spec in the Docs tab that told operators to check a detached exit code with `cat`, which judges `cat`. And the drift: seven rows in the last round were already closed and this file had not caught up, describing a system worse than the one that exists.

sections.heading: Why this page exists, and what a status means on it
sections.body:
A requirement and a gap are the same object seen from two sides. The six pages beside this one document 88 gaps precisely and never say what any of them was supposed to be doing. `The fence is not enforced at the resource` is only legible next to `a fenced holder must not be able to reach the device`.

So this page is the other side: every requirement this system has been given, functional and non-functional, with where it came from, whether it holds today, and the check that decided it. Statuses were verified against the code, not copied from the commit that claimed them — several rows below disagree with the message that raised them.

Two structural facts several rows depend on. **The demo is not the system**: `internal/demo` writes `farm.device_runtime`, `farm.recovery_attempts`, `farm.quarantines`, `farm.events` and `farm.jobs.state` with its own rules, so a row it wrote proves the schema works and proves nothing about the loop whose job it is. And **nothing runs as its own Postgres role**: `farm_reaper`, `farm_scheduler` and `farm_watchdog` are created `NOLOGIN` and every process connects with one `DATABASE_URL`.
bullets: **Origins** are cited as `c:<sha>` for a commit, `gap:<area>.<n>` for entry *n* of that area page's `gaps` array, `schema` when the migration is the contract, `cap:features` for an entry in `featureStatuses()`, and `research:*` for an external finding.
An ID names where a requirement **lives**, not where it is violated: the fence-at-the-resource requirement is `SEC-04` even though its absence is felt in the lease protocol.
The full register, with the long-form evidence for every row, is `REQUIREMENTS.md` at the repository root. This page is that file rendered where an operator already is.

rows: Implemented, and demonstrated to work. The only status that means stop reading.
Implemented, with a named hole. The row names it.
Nothing in the tree implements it.
Implemented, reachable only on Linux — and not reachable in any deployment that ships today.
Implemented and plausibly correct, never observed working.
Raised, answered by a decision rather than by code. No implementation is owed.

sections.heading: Last re-verified: against HEAD, 2026-09-06 — 86 of 101 met, one row open
sections.body:
Against `HEAD`, 2026-09-06, after forty-four branches. **Eighty-six rows are
`met` outright**, eleven more are `met` in one dimension, three are `decided`,
and **one is open**.

### The one open row

`REC-03` — tiers 3 and 4 against real hardware. `HW-05` is the same sentence
about a narrower thing. There is no phone attached to the machine this was
built on, and no amount of further code changes that: `USBDEVFS_RESET` has
never been issued against a handset, and `uhubctl` has never cut VBUS on a
hub. Everything leading to those two calls is written, tested, and has now been
RUN on Linux — `scripts/linux-acceptance.sh` starts `farmd node` against a
sysfs-shaped tree on a real filesystem, and discovery reads a hub's per-port
switchability from the kernel's own file mode on each port's `disable`. Reading
that a port CAN be switched is not switching it, and this register will not
pretend otherwise.

### What moved, and why sixteen rows moved at once

Sixteen rows closed in this round, and they divide into two kinds that are worth
keeping apart.

**Seven were already closed and the register had not caught up.** `LEASE-14`
was fixed by `00007`'s ledger trigger; `DEV-02` by `00011`'s rewrite of rung 3;
`DEV-07` when all thirteen topology knobs were wired; `API-07` when `ctl` began
posting to `/specs/validate`; `SEC-03` when the identity started reaching
`farm.audit_log`; `JOB-08` when the step routes were mounted; and half of
`LEASE-10` when the alert and its runbook shipped. Their evidence cited code
that had been replaced, in one case three migrations earlier. A register that is
only ever revised downward is not being checked, and this one had been drifting
upward — describing a system worse than the one that exists — for long enough
that a reader would have distrusted the rows that were still true.

**Nine were closed by work in this round**, and three of those were not on
anybody's list until an agent went looking:

- **`SEC-05` was open by a door nobody had tried.** The lease listing was clean,
  but `00009` wrote `prior_instance` and `new_instance` into a
  `lease_reattached` event, and `GET /api/v1/events` projected `detail`
  verbatim — republishing `lease_id` + `fence` + `holder_instance` in one
  record, to an operator token that is unscoped across every tenant, and into
  the dashboard timeline. The comment in `internal/api/leases.go` that skipped a
  tenant check on renew was *justifying itself* on the claim this broke.
- **`JOB-03` was narrower than recorded and its documented remedy did not
  work.** The exit status was read at launch and on re-attach; a soak that died
  at hour four was still green. And the reference spec shipped in the Docs tab
  told operators to check it with `cat …result` and `expect_exit: [0]`, which
  judges `cat`.
- **`JOB-10` was in direct tension with a sibling requirement**, and nothing
  arbitrated. `TestABookkeepingFailureIsNeverAVerdictOnTheJob` pins that a
  swallowed write is not a verdict; `JOB-10` forbids the `succeeded` that
  produces. The resolution is to WITHHOLD the verdict rather than downgrade it:
  the job keeps `running`, which is the absence of a verdict, so both hold.

### What the round is actually worth

Fourteen units landed as fourteen PRs, and the number that matters is not that.
It is that **four separate defects were found by running the thing rather than
by reading it**, and every one was invisible to a green suite:

- Every role panicked at startup on a duplicate metrics registration, while
  `go build`, `go vet`, `gofmt` and the whole suite stayed green — because
  nothing called `newRegistry`. Found by starting the binary on Linux.
- `topo.Sysfs` had never executed: all eighteen topology tests hand `FromFS` an
  `fstest.MapFS`, and the shipped binary reads through `os.DirFS`, taking a
  hub's switchability from a file MODE a MapFS can only assert into being.
- The dashboard never receives a live stream on any farm with tokens set,
  because `EventSource` cannot send headers. Found while adding a column to it.
- The schema had only ever been checked against one PostgreSQL major.

And three tests were found to be passing for the wrong reason — one asserting on
`encoding/json` instead of the code under test, one matching the wrong line of
the file it scanned, one whose clock made its own falsification undetectable.
All three were written in this session, by the same process that then caught
them. That is what the falsify-every-assertion rule is for, and it earned its
cost four times over.

Every moved row names the file, migration or live observation that moved it, so
a reader can re-run the check rather than trust the verdict.

sections.heading: The founding requirement
sections.body:
One requirement produced this system, and it came from somebody else's incident: DeviceFarmer/STF issue #663, open and unanswered since 2023. A device running automation gets an `ECONNRESET` after about ninety minutes and is automatically released mid-run, destroying hours of work.

The requirement is not `handle transport failures gracefully`. It is that the failure must be **unrepresentable**. A lease ends when the job says so, when a written-down deadline elapses, or when a human takes it back — and there is no fourth way to write it down.

examples.label: The requirement, as a CHECK constraint
examples.note: Seven values, none of them connectivity-flavoured. `released because the transport dropped` cannot be spelled. This is LEASE-01, and it is the one requirement in the register that is enforced in four independent places rather than one.

sections.heading: LEASE — the lease protocol
sections.body: Fourteen requirements: the invariant itself and everything that protects it. Six hold outright. The interesting failures are not the missing features — they are the two places where a protection exists in DDL that no deployment assumes (`LEASE-03`), and where a second automatic ending exists that none of the reaper's controls reach (`LEASE-08`).

rows: A lease ends when the job says so, when a written-down deadline elapses, or when a human takes it back. Never because of connectivity.
`farm.leases.release_reason` is CHECK-constrained to seven values with no connectivity term (`migrations/00001_core.sql`). The failure is unrepresentable, not handled.
Lease liveness, job liveness and device health are three clocks, separated by table, by function and by Postgres role.

`farm.leases` and `farm.device_runtime` are distinct tables with distinct writers; `internal/watchdog` has no lease write path; `internal/obs.TransportBlip` takes no lease identifier and returns nothing, so transport code has no value to branch on.
Reclamation must be structurally unable to read device health.

`FARM_DB_ROLE` makes a process assume the role. `openPool` (`cmd/farmd/roles.go`) runs `SET ROLE` in `AfterConnect`, once per physical connection, and refuses at startup when the login user is not a member. `migrations/00015_runtime_roles.sql` grants `farm_reaper`, `farm_scheduler` and `farm_watchdog` to the login user and completes the grants each loop needs to run WHOLE. Proven, not asserted: `test/assertions_v15.sql` runs the reaper's entire pass as `farm_reaper` (R1 shows `SELECT` on `farm.device_runtime` raising `insufficient_privilege`) and the watchdog's as `farm_watchdog` (W1 shows the same on `farm.leases`), and Z1 shows that whole pass ending no lease. It is opt-in per process and refused for `all` and `demo`, because one pool serving six roles cannot assume one role.
The witness cap counts only *consecutive* witness-only extensions, so a renew resets it.
`migrations/00002_lease.sql:358`. Without it a job expires 12 minutes into any run that witnesses once.
A control-plane outage is refunded to the tenant, computed across every component on the renewal path.

`migrations/00012_reaper_arm_unbeaten.sql` rewrites `farm.reaper_arm` to `unnest` the watch list and LEFT JOIN the heartbeats, so a component with no row is visible instead of dropping out of the `min()`. It returns `TABLE(armed, gap, unbeaten)`; a watched name that has never beaten refuses the arm, writes `reaper_state.last_refusal`, and nothing is reclaimed until it beats. Verified live on the demo: `farm.reaper_arm(ARRAY['reaper','api','ghost_component'], '60s')` returns `f | 00:00:00 | {ghost_component}` and the refusal text names the component and says why silence cannot be told from an outage. `test/assertions_v12.sql` and `test/assertions_v15.sql` (R3, R7) cover both directions.
Every mutating lease function matches on `(id, fence)`, so a stale holder's write is rejected in the database.
`migrations/00002_lease.sql`; `test/assertions.sql` proves the pod-eviction re-attach at an unchanged fence.
A zero-row renew (fenced, terminal) must never be conflated with a transient database error (retry).

`internal/lease/holder.go` distinguishes `ErrFenced` from a transient error, and the API distinguishes 410 from 503. The branch its own doc comment calls "the single most consequential decision in this project" has no test: the `leaseOps` interface exists so a stub can drive it, and nothing does. `gap:lease.6`
The `max_runtime` sweep must fence the ended holder and rearm its slot, as release and reclaim do.

`farm.lease_expire_max_runtime` raises `devices.fence_floor` from `farm.fence_seq` and sets `slots.rearm_at` (`migrations/00005_correctness.sql:389`), so a max_runtime ending fences and rearms exactly as release and reclaim do. The rewrite had to `DROP FUNCTION` the one-argument form first: `CREATE OR REPLACE` matches on the argument list, so adding `p_rearm` created an overload and the Go call became ambiguous (42725). Whether the sweep should also answer to the kill switch is LEASE-11, not this row — `max_runtime` is a deadline the user wrote down, which the founding requirement names as a legitimate ending.
A job that is demonstrably alive on the device but blind to the control plane can extend its lease (witness).

The jobrunner starts a marker and a witness loop for every placement (`internal/jobrunner/witness.go`, called from `runJob`), and the three cadences derive from `FARM_LEASE_WITNESS_INTERVAL` by one rule that `New` refuses to have set by hand. A marker that cannot be built does not refuse the placement — the job runs on ttl+grace and `farm_jobrunner_witnessless_total` counts it — because refusing here would turn a missing safeguard into the harm it exists to prevent. Proven live on 2026-09-05 with `FARM_LEASE_WITNESS_INTERVAL=30s` and a 100-second step: lease placed at 17:19:08, `farm.leases.witness_at` set at 17:19:38 with `witness_extensions=1`, `reclaimable_at` pushed to 18:04:08, and `farm_jobrunner_witness_total{outcome="accepted"} 1`.
A protected lease is never auto-reclaimed; it is held and a human is paged.

The guard has been in `farm.lease_reclaim` since `00012` (`AND l.protected = false  -- hold and page instead`), and the paging is real: `farm_lease_suspect{protected="true"}` is pre-seeded so it exists before the first casualty, `DeviceFarmerProtectedLeaseSuspect` reads it, and `docs/runbooks/protected-lease-suspect.md` says what to do. What was missing was a test that could fail. `test/assertions_protected_lease.sql` INSERTs a protected suspect lease with deadlines already past — legal because `leases_guard` is BEFORE UPDATE only — beside an identical UNPROTECTED sibling, and asserts the control was reclaimed and the protected one was not. Without the control, "nothing was reclaimed" also means "nothing was reclaimable". Falsified: deleting the guard leaves every other suite green and fails this one alone. `test/e2e/reaper_test.go` proves the same against the real reaper process, in 0.25s.
The automatic release path has an operator-reachable kill switch.

`GET /api/v1/reaper`, `POST /api/v1/reaper/disable` and `/enable` are operator routes (`internal/api/reaper_admin.go`), each requiring a reason and writing `farm.audit_log`; `ctl reaper [disable|enable --reason r]` drives them. `max_runtime` deliberately does NOT answer the switch: it is a deadline the USER wrote down, which the founding invariant names as a legitimate ending. The switch is for RECLAMATION — an ending the user did not write — and the endpoint's own note says so.

`cmd/farmd/roles.go` builds `jobrunner.Config` with `HolderConfig{Interval: cfg.Lease.RenewInterval}`, so the value validated at startup is the value the holder renews on. Before this the startup assertion guaranteeing three renewals inside the TTL was guarding a number no holder read.
`FARM_REAPER_COMPONENTS` cannot be set to something that fuses the health clock into the lease clock.

`internal/config` now refuses a `FARM_REAPER_COMPONENTS` carrying a health-plane component, with a deny list derived from `roleComponents` filtered by `!onRenewalPath` so a component added to a role is refused the day it is added. It is a deny list and not `!onRenewalPath(name)` because the latter would break the legitimate renames the existing guard exists for (`api-canary`, `scheduler-a`). A second guard catches the case a name list cannot: a watchdog RENAMED to `wd` beats as `wd:h01`, a name that has a heartbeat row, and the reaper's config cannot know what another process was renamed to — so the refusal is made on the process that owns the rename. Refuses to BOOT, on every role. The stakes are in the message: `00012:119-129` extends every live lease by the gap and pushes `quiesce_until`, so a watchdog outage would move every deadline in the farm.
The way a lease ended is recoverable from an event log at 3am.

`migrations/00007_lease_events.sql` installs `farm.trg_leases_ledger()`, an AFTER UPDATE OF state trigger whose `WHEN` covers all four ending paths because each writes `state` in the same UPDATE, writing one `lease_ended` row with `release_reason`, `ended_by`, `terminal_state`, `held_seconds`, `heartbeat_age_s` and the witness columns — in the same transaction as the ending, plus the view `farm.v_lease_endings`. The register's evidence ("0 lease_released events") predated that migration. What was missing was a reader: `GET /api/v1/leases/endings`, `GET /api/v1/leases/{id}/ending` and `ctl endings` serve it now, and `00018` grants SELECT on the view to `farm_reaper` while REVOKING it by name from `farm_watchdog` and `farm_parker` — a view is read with its OWNER's rights, so granting this one to the watchdog would reopen the #663 firewall through a view-shaped hole without touching a single grant on `farm.leases`.

sections.heading: DEV — device identity, topology and health
sections.body:
Twelve requirements. The identity model is the strongest thing in the system and the enrollment loop that would exercise it has never run, anywhere, for a reason that is one guard in `runNode` (`OPS-04`).

`DEV-09` is the sharpest row in the register: a fleet whose fire mitigation is charge limiting and early thermal detection (`HW-03`) has a schema column for each and collects neither.

rows: Every call that targets a physical position is addressed by USB devpath, never by serial.

`internal/adbwire` has zero internal dependencies and a test that fails the build if allocation vocabulary appears anywhere in it — it caught a comment its own author wrote. A clone test asserts a devpath-addressed command reaches exactly one of two devices sharing `0123456789ABCDEF`.
One function owns "is this the device we think it is", resolving strongest evidence first: brand, fingerprint, serial-and-slot, adopt.

The register described `00005`'s body; the live definition is `00011`. Rung 3 no longer parks its verdict in `v_res` — ambiguity has its own carrier (`v_amb`), because `v_res` is what each rung overwrites — and rung 4 re-checks AFTER the INSERT, which is the case the register's scenario actually hits: the second clone of a duplicated serial sees `count = 1` at its own lookup, so the collision is only visible post-insert. Covered non-trivially by `test/assertions_v11.sql` V2, V5 and V6.
A device sharing a serial with another is flagged durably, not just logged.

`farm.resolve_device` (`migrations/00011_resolve_ambiguous.sql`) writes `farm.devices.serial_ambiguous` on BOTH rows of a clone pair, and the next pass resolves each by brand. Now covered: `internal/enroll` has 24 tests over `Probe`, `HardwareFingerprint`, `parseProps` and `Brander.Read/Brand/Rebrand` against `test/fakeadb`, including `TwoClonesFixture`, plus `EnrollOnce` against a scratch database exercising adoption, re-sighting and the ambiguous case; `internal/topo` has 18 over `FromFS(fstest.MapFS)`, the hub plan and the labeller. `internal/adbwire/device.go`'s doc no longer credits the watchdog with a write it never made.
A handset plugged into a host joins the fleet without a human writing SQL.

The enrollment loop ran on Linux against a live ADB server and took every branch of its decision tree without a line of SQL from a human: it adopted a device whose serial another row already claimed and said so loudly ("ADOPTED a device on CONTESTED evidence … a human should confirm the two are really different handsets"), recorded sightings and adopted nothing for two offline handsets and for seven attached at positions discovery had not registered, and reported `0 known, 0 adopted, 2 unreadable, 7 pending, 5 ambiguous`. The ADB server was `test/fakeadb`, not a phone, so the wire is proved and the handset is not.
A host reports its USB tree and the controller, hub, power domain and slot rows grow to fit.
`met` in code; `unverified` against a kernel-populated tree

`topo.Sysfs` — the `os.DirFS` path the shipped binary takes, which no test had ever executed, because all 18 topo tests hand `FromFS` an `fstest.MapFS` — ran on Linux against a sysfs-shaped tree on a real filesystem and wrote one hub (7 ports), seven slots labelled `R1-U40-H3.1-P1..P7`, and one `per_port` power domain controlled by `uhubctl` at `3-1`. It skipped the root hub, as the filter says it should. `vbus_switchable=true` came from the real file MODE (0644) on each port's `disable` file — the one thing a MapFS can only assert into being, since it is the kernel's stat that decides whether a port can be switched. The tree was written by a script rather than by a kernel enumerating hardware, which is the remaining gap.
A hub without per-port switching gets ONE ganged power domain, so the ladder cannot cycle seven devices to fix one.

`farm.power_domains` models what one switch controls, and the seed now gives a `per_port` hub one domain PER PORT and a ganged hub exactly one (`internal/demo/seed.go`). Before this the demo gave every hub a single domain whatever its hardware, so tier 4's blast radius was seven ports on per-port hardware and a neighbour's `no_disruption` lease refused a cycle that would physically have disturbed one. Verified live: `ctl slot list --host h01` shows `per_port (uhubctl)` per position.
A slot is marked, never deleted, and a hub that vanishes is reconciled.

All thirteen `topo.Config` fields reach the binary through `FARM_TOPO_*`, validated and printed by `Summary()`; `reconcileRemovals` is reachable, applies its mass-removal bound, and marks rather than deletes (`state = 'maintenance'` with a `slot_vanished` event and an audit row in one transaction). `RetireVanished` defaults OFF and that is a documented decision, stated in three places: the first pass a new deployment runs is against a host whose slots were seeded by hand, with USB paths that may not match what the scan sees, and reconciliation would retire the lot — the mass-removal bound catches most of that, and a host with one seeded slot is under it. What remains is operational, not code: an out-of-the-box deployment leaves a vanished port as an active empty slot until an operator turns the knob on.
An operator can register a slot, re-slot a device or rebrand one without hand-written SQL.

`internal/api/slots.go` serves `GET /api/v1/slots`, `POST /api/v1/slots` (`farm.register_slot`), `POST /slots/{id}/label`, `POST /devices/{id}/reslot` and `/rebrand`; `migrations/00017_reslot.sql` adds `farm.reslot_device` and `farm.relabel_slot` with an occupancy check and an audit row. Every verb is operator-gated, requires a reason, and refuses while the device holds a live lease — nothing here can end one. `ctl slot list|register|label|reslot|rebrand` drives them; `test/assertions_v17.sql` covers the SQL. Verified live: `ctl slot list --host h01`.
Battery state of charge, battery temperature and the charge gate are collected per device.

Collected and now acted on. `migrations/00016_battery_readings.sql` adds `farm.battery_readings` with a retention function, the watchdog writes the series beside the columns, and `internal/watchdog/swell.go` flags a temperature rise, an absolute ceiling and an idle-drain rate as `farm.events` kind `battery_anomaly` carrying `rack_slot`, because a human walks to a position. `internal/chargepolicy` holds idle devices inside a 40–80% band. `test/assertions_v16.sql` covers the schema.
Health is a token bucket, not a raw counter, so a device cannot flap between healthy and quarantined on every blip.

One damper, in one place: `internal/watchdog/damper.go` owns the token bucket (cap 10, refill 1/min) and `watchdog.DamperSQL` is the single statement both the watchdog and the simulator run, so the demo can no longer show hysteresis the product does not have. The simulator also honours `suppress_until` now and opens recovery attempts with it set, as the real ladder does, so an induced transport drop is no longer fed back to the observer as evidence of a broken phone.
The ADB host protocol and the sync (file transfer) protocol are spoken natively, with no shelling out to `adb`.

`internal/adbwire/sync_list.go` speaks `LIST`/`DENT` natively (`SyncConn.List`) and `Client.MkdirAll` creates a push's parent directory with a validated path; `test/fakeadb` answers `LIST`. Nothing shells out to `adb`. `internal/runner/steps.go` creates the parent before a push, and after a failure that aborts a job every remaining step is written to `farm.job_steps` as `skipped` with a reason, so the job's step list is complete rather than trailing off.
The health plane can never touch a lease.
`REVOKE ALL ON farm.leases FROM farm_watchdog`, plus the Go import barrier. See LEASE-03 for why the first half binds nothing at runtime; the second half holds.

sections.heading: JOB — the step model, execution and configuration
sections.body:
Twelve requirements. `JOB-02` is the thesis of the project and it works, observed repeatedly. Most of the rest describe a job that can be filed but not configured, not validated, and not read back afterwards.

The pattern worth naming: three separate rows (`JOB-05`, `JOB-06`, `JOB-11`) are cases where the mechanism is fully written and the one call site or one column write that would activate it is missing. None is a design problem.

rows: The step vocabulary is closed and the database owns it, so a spec written today means the same thing when it resumes tomorrow.
`farm.step_kinds` carries the ten kinds and the idempotent flag a resume needs. `TestKindTableMatchesMigration` pins the Go vocabulary to the migration and fails if they drift.
A transport failure inside a step is retried inside the lease, with no attempt cap, bounded only by a deadline the job's author wrote down.

Observed end to end: a job survived 8 ADB transport blips across 4 renewals and completed all 10 steps; a later run survived six transport failures inside the lease that held them. This is the thesis, and it is the one that works.
Long work runs detached on the device so no socket is the source of truth.

A detached run's exit status was read at launch and on re-attach, and nowhere else — so a soak that started cleanly and exited 137 four hours later produced a green step AND a green `wait_for`, because `execWaitFor` judged the operator's probe and the canonical probe is `test -f …result`. `jobspec.WaitFor` now takes a `handle` naming a `shell_detached` step declared earlier in the same spec, and `execWaitForDetached` polls that run's status through the same `probeDetached` a re-attach uses. The probe form is untouched, so no existing spec changes meaning. `running` is no longer inferred from the log file — which nothing removes, so a worker killed from outside looked identical to a soak in its third hour — but from the pid file checked against `/proc`, deliberately not `kill -0`, which cannot tell a dead process from a shell lacking signal 0. Falsified differentially: one device, one status sequence, both forms — the probe form passes a killed soak, the handle form catches it. The demo's soak spec, the README's front-door spec and `jobs.json`'s reference spec all taught the broken pattern and were rewritten; `cat …result` with `expect_exit: [0]` judges `cat`.
A job checkpoints and resumes, re-running nothing whose side effect would repeat.

`planResume`'s decisions were covered by nine tests on hand-built `Checkpoint` literals; the round trip they depend on — `saveCheckpoint` → `farm.jobs.checkpoint` jsonb → `parseCheckpoint` → `belongsTo` → `planResume` — had never run, and `saveCheckpoint` had no test at all, including the fence guard that stops a zombie holder overwriting the progress of the attempt that replaced it. `internal/runner/checkpoint_db_test.go` drives `Runner.Run` TWICE against one job with an eviction in between, against a real database and without adding a seam to make it testable. Falsified: relaxing the fence guard fails with `a holder at fence 7 overwrote the progress of the attempt at fence 8`; ignoring `plan.skip` fails with `the replacement re-ran a step that had already finished`.
A spec is validated before a device is allocated to it.

`specSubmissionError` has a caller — `internal/api/jobs_submit.go:215` — so the gate its own doc comment describes is applied before a job is filed, and the seven jobs that failed with `jobspec: invalid spec` after each burning an attempt on a different real device are no longer reachable. The expensive half (the rule set) was always written; this row existed because the cheap half was not.
A reset tier expands into a real step list from the job's profile, so reset is generic.

`internal/api/jobs_submit.go` writes `profile_id`, `reset_tier`, `max_attempts` and `resumable` from the submission, and a reset expands against the job's profile. This row said `not_built in practice` against a tree that already had it; the check is `ctl submit --profile`.
The per-job knobs the runner reads are settable when the job is filed.
Same code path as JOB-06: every per-job knob the runner reads is settable at submission and reaches `farm.jobs`. Corrected here rather than built.
An operator can see which step failed, and what it printed, without a database session.

`GET /api/v1/jobs/{id}/steps` and `/attempts` are served from `internal/api/jobsteps.go` and mounted through `api.WithRoutes`, carrying `State`, `ExitCode`, `Output`, `Error` and `Detail`, with `OutputChars`/`OutputTruncated`/`OutputOmitted` so a cut log never reads as an empty one; `ctl job steps` renders the failing step's output. All three residuals are closed too: 605 lines of read surface that nothing asserted now have `jobsteps_test.go`, including the truncation budget tuned against measured 144 MB responses; the SSE digest carries the current step, excluding `skipped` tails and `continue_on_error` failures from the failure rank because neither is where the job IS; and the dashboard has a Steps panel.
A step or attempt row whose process died is closed by something.

`internal/janitor` is the sweeper. It closes ORPHANS ONLY, keyed on the LEASE being dead rather than on the step being slow — the distinction is the whole design, because a six-hour `shell_detached` step is exactly what this system is for, and sweeping it for looking stale would be #663 wearing a different hat. `job_steps_live` finally has a query that uses it, and the rows that poisoned the jobrunner's claim predicate resolve.
A job's reported state agrees with its step rows.

A job reached `succeeded` without anything consulting its step rows, and two branches never recorded the steps they skipped, so a `max_runtime` abort left no rows at all for the remainder. Both branches record now, and a guard before `writeJobState(…, "succeeded")` asks `farm.job_steps` — not the loop's own counters — whether the rows account for the whole spec. The verdict is WITHHELD rather than downgraded, which is what makes this compatible with `TestABookkeepingFailureIsNeverAVerdictOnTheJob`: nothing is written, the job keeps `'running'` — the ABSENCE of a verdict — so a swallowed bookkeeping write still decides nothing about the job, and `succeeded` is still never claimed without evidence. The operator gets an ERROR line, a reason on `farm.jobs.error`, and a `job_success_not_asserted` event; the janitor places the job again. `sweepUnevidencedSuccess` covers terminal jobs, which the old sweep could not see — it was bounded by `state = 'running'`.

`farm.device_matches` and `farm.selector_unknown_keys` land in `migrations/00005_correctness.sql:159`, and `lease_acquire` filters on `farm.device_matches(d.id, j.selector)` in both allocation queries. A selector key the schema does not support is now an exception naming the supported keys, rather than a filter that silently matches everything — a job asking for `{"model":"Pixel 7"}` used to get whatever was next in the failure-score ordering.
A payload cannot lie about its kind, and an unrunnable spec cannot be accepted unchecked.

Found by running it: both `Shell` and `*Shell` satisfied `Payload` because `Kind()` has a value receiver, and the pointer form **skipped every validation rule**. Both paths now normalise, with a regression test that fails if the rules stop firing. `Kind()` on a typed nil also panicked, which would have crashed an API handler validating somebody's submission.

sections.heading: REC — recovery, blast radius and quarantine
sections.body:
Thirteen requirements. The refusal contract — a rung whose blast radius exceeds what a live lease permits is refused and recorded, never quietly downgraded — is the part of this system most worth keeping, and it is implemented correctly.

What is missing is everything downstream of it: two of nine rungs cannot execute, refusals from one path are not queryable as refusals, and the operator action most likely to be taken before physical work — draining a host — writes a column the allocator has never read.

rows: Tiers are stored, not hard-coded, each with a blast radius and the minimum lease disruption policy it requires.
`farm.recovery_tiers`. The Docs tab renders the ladder from the table, so a new rung appears without an edit.
A rung whose blast radius exceeds what a live lease permits is refused and the refusal recorded, never quietly downgraded.

`internal/recovery` reads `farm.leases` in exactly one function, only to decide whether it is allowed to act, and writes none. On this demo the ladder's per-device escalation path has never executed: of 48 refusal rows, 37 were written by the simulator, 11 by the API slot-power handler, and 0 by the ladder. `gap:devices.10`, `gap:recovery.17`
Tiers 3 (USBDEVFS_RESET) and 4 (VBUS power) execute against real hardware.

`runRecovery` builds a `node.Client` over `node.NewDBResolver(pool)` when `FARM_NODE_TOKEN` is set and hands it to the actuator, so tiers 3 and 4 reach `POST /node/v1/usb-reset` and `/node/v1/port-power` rather than a nil runner refusing them. The agent on the far end has now been RUN on Linux — `scripts/linux-acceptance.sh` starts `farmd node` against a sysfs-shaped tree on a real filesystem and checks what discovery wrote — but `USBDEVFS_RESET` has never been issued against a handset. That is the whole of what is left, and it needs a phone.
A rung that cannot run is refused with a reason naming what is missing, rather than reported as ineffective.

`recovery.Record` is still the one place a `Result` becomes `outcome` and `refusal`, and the verdict now GOVERNS the ladder as well as describing it: `Disposition.Escalate()` decides whether the rung was spent, so a refusal or an unreachable host leaves `ladder_tier` where it was and a dead host no longer reads as a dead handset. One classifier serves both callers — `recovery.ClassifyHostFault`, which the actuator's rung-bound method is a thin wrapper over — so the operator's slot-power route files rows the ladder's reader cannot tell from its own, and a ganged refusal carries `detail.refusal_kind` whichever path produced it.
A refusal is queryable as a refusal.

`Record(res)` is now the one place that turns an actuator `Result` into the two columns `farm.recovery_attempts` keeps, and it preserves what the actuator worked hardest to establish. The switch it replaced folded anything unrecognised into `OutcomeFailed`, so a REFUSAL (this rung is not permitted here — the device is fine) and an UNREACHABLE host (no rung will help until somebody fixes the host) both read as "the hardware failed": a dead host looked like a dead phone, and the ladder quarantined handsets that were never broken while spending cooldown budget on a machine that had gone away. `WHERE outcome = 'refused'` now finds refusals.
Several devices failing together on one hub is ONE incident, not N.

`farm.v_hub_health` is the correlation and hub-scoped quarantine is the action. But `farm.v_fleet` joins quarantines on `device_id`, which is NULL for hub- and host-scoped rows, so the grid shows a quarantined device with no explanation; and the view's `unhealthy` (`NOT IN ('healthy','retired')`) is a different definition from the ladder's (`offline, unauthorized, missing, degraded`), so the banner and the quarantine reason report different counts on the same hub. `gap:recovery.7`, `gap:recovery.8`, `gap:devices.13`
Draining a host stops new leases landing on it.

`farm.lease_acquire` joins `farm.hosts` and requires `h.admin_state = 'enabled'` in both allocation queries (`migrations/00005_correctness.sql:226`). The allocator had been filtering the DEVICE's `admin_state` and never the host's, so `POST /hosts/{id}/drain` answered "no new leases will be placed on this host" and then placed them — measured live at seven new leases on a drained host inside sixty seconds.
Closing a quarantine returns its devices to the pool.

`POST /api/v1/quarantines/{id}/close` finishes the release in the SAME transaction as the close: `farm.device_runtime.health` to `unknown` with `ladder_tier = 0`, and `farm.devices.admin_state` out of `quarantined`, for every covered device no other open quarantine still covers. It answers with `devices_released` and `devices_reenabled` — counts, because an operator who frees nothing has learned something. A farm-wide advisory lock serialises closes, since two operators closing overlapping quarantines under READ COMMITTED would each see the other's row open and neither would release the device. The coverage test reads `scope`, not the subject columns: a `scope='device'` row carries `host_id` too, so the old predicate made one broken phone read as a quarantine over its whole host. Verified live: a hub quarantine over 7 devices closed to `unknown|enabled|7` immediately, with no recovery cycle in between. `reconcileQuarantines` remains the backstop for rows closed by other means.
Quarantine can be scoped to the granularity of the actual fault.

`migrations/00014_quarantine_power_domain.sql` adds `farm.quarantines.power_domain_id` with a partial unique index, and `coveredByQuarantine` gains the arm; `POST /api/v1/quarantines` accepts `scope ∈ device|slot|hub|host|power_domain` and `ctl quarantine open --scope` drives it. `test/assertions_v14.sql` proves a `power_domain` quarantine covers every slot of the domain and that closing it releases only the devices no other open quarantine still covers. A human parking a device beats the automation (`device_park` with `p_auto=false`).
The ladder's first action on a settled unhealthy device is the cheapest rung.

`ladder_tier` now names the lowest rung still UNSPENT rather than the one just spent, so the column default of 0 means "observe first" and tier 0 is selected on the first attempt. See `rungAfter` and the `>=` in `next` (`internal/recovery/ladder.go:487`). Before this the table advertised a rung that never ran and a budget never spent, and every incident opened one rung more aggressive than the ladder claimed.
An action recorded as an open recovery attempt is closed by whoever performs it.

`handleSlotPower` performs the cycle synchronously through the same `node.Client` the ladder uses — `PortPowerWithDomain`, resolved per host from `farm.hosts.node_endpoint` — and closes its own row with `recovery.FinishAttempt` carrying the real outcome. With no agent configured it answers 503 saying so and opens NO row, rather than a `requested` line the janitor aborts fifteen minutes later. The response is 200 with the result, not 202. It takes an advisory lock per slot and sets `device_id` so the ladder's in-flight check covers it.
Bulk selection does not sweep up devices that are quarantined or unhealthy.

Health and quarantine are exclusions in `expandBulkSelector` now, with `include_unhealthy` and `include_quarantined` to opt back in — two flags rather than one, because wanting to shell into a degraded handset is not asking to interrupt a recovery cycle.
Recovery history is queryable by the questions an operator actually asks.

`GET /api/v1/recovery` narrows by `outcome`, `tier` (number or name), `hub` (id or `usb_path`) and `since` (RFC3339 or a duration such as `2h`), on top of `device`, `host` and `limit`. A value that can match nothing is a 400 naming the parameter, not an empty list. The `since` interval is sent as a duration so the clock that anchors it is the server's. `ctl recovery --outcome --tier --hub --since` asks the same question from a terminal. Verified live: `GET /api/v1/recovery?outcome=refused&tier=4&since=2h` → 200.

sections.heading: API — the HTTP surface, the CLI and artifacts
sections.body:
Nine requirements. The envelope and the status-code discipline are right, and `API-01` matters more than it looks: conflating 410 fenced with 503 transient is STF #663 reached through a different door.

`API-03` is the one with deployment consequences. The artifact path works only because the runner and the API share a disk, so it does not survive the split-role deployment the compose file's own `farm` profile describes.

rows: Every non-2xx body is one envelope, and 410 fenced (abort) is distinguishable from 503 transient (lease untouched).
Conflating those two is STF #663 with a different trigger, and the two codes carry that distinction all the way to `internal/lease`.
The role an endpoint needs is chosen at registration, not inside the handler, so no endpoint can exist without a level.

`buildHandler` now wraps every route in `tenant(...)` or `operator(...)`; the one bare `mux.HandleFunc` under `/api/v1/` is gone. The invariant as written in `Handler`'s doc comment and restated on the Interfaces page — the level is chosen at registration, so no endpoint can exist without one — now holds without an exception to explain.
The Docs reference recovers from a transient fetch failure.

A failed area fetch is cached with `retryable: true` and rendered with a **Try again** button that drops the entry and refetches (`internal/ui/assets/docs.js`). Only a FAILURE is dropped: discarding a loaded area would refetch a document that is already correct. Before this, a page opened while the api was restarting kept its error for the life of the tab, because the area was in the cache and `ensureArea` returned on its first line.
An artifact's bytes are fetchable over HTTP, so roles can be split across hosts.

`ArtifactAPI.RegisterBlobRoutes` mounts the content route and `cmd/farmd/roles.go:306` calls it. A farm could previously store a 200MB APK it could not hand back, with the blob store as the only copy, and the runner worked solely because it shared a disk with the API — so the artifact path did not survive the split-role deployment the compose file describes. `internal/api/method_test.go` checks the bytes hash to the name they were fetched under, which is the assertion that would catch a store serving the wrong artifact.
Disk under the artifact directory is reclaimable.

`cmd/farmd/roles.go` mounts `api.NewBlobGC(...)` beside the blob routes with the grace from `FARM_ARTIFACT_GC_GRACE` (floor `MinArtifactGCGrace`, mirrored from `api.MinBlobGCGrace` so a process that would be refused does not finish booting). `ctl artifacts gc [--apply]` and `artifacts delete <sha> --reason` drive it. Verified live: a dry run reported 4 blobs, 786 B scanned, 1 entry not filed as a digest and never touched, 0 referenced. Nothing sweeps unless an operator asks.
A method mismatch returns 405 with an `Allow` header.

`internal/api/method.go` reconstructs the method mismatch that the catch-all under `/api/v1/` made unreachable, and answers 405 with an `Allow` header. The negative case is the one that mattered and it is tested: reconstructing it must NOT turn a typo'd URL into a 405, because that advertises routes which do not exist. Telling a client the resource is missing when the resource is fine made a generic client retry a verb error as a vanished device.
`ctl` exit codes distinguish "the control plane failed" from "a target failed".

`ctl bulk` returns 4 through `ErrPartial`, and the two single-target verbs that still conflated a target failure with a control-plane failure now do too: a phone that exits non-zero and a power cycle that finished `failed`/`aborted` are both 4, not 1. Proved with process exit statuses from the shipped binary, not unit tests: exec with the phone exiting 7 → 4; power `failed` → 4; a dead port → 1; a 409 on a leased device → 3. One case was found while fixing it — `adbwire.DrainShellV2` leaves `ExitCode:-1, Exited:false` when the shell stream ends with no exit frame, and turning that into 4 would tell a script the run completed when the command may still be running; `execOutcome` reads `res.Exited` first.
`ctl` validates against the server, which is the authority.

`ctl submit` and `ctl validate` post to `/api/v1/specs/validate`, and `ctl kinds`/`ctl resets` fetch the other two; `cmdSpecValidate` prints which server checked it. The superseded local path — `cmdSubmit`, `cmdValidate` and the five helpers only they used — is deleted rather than left as a second authority for the next reader to find, and the package doc no longer claims `ctl validate` "never leaves the machine".

Answered by deleting it. `cmd/farmd/main.go` documents why there is no code 3: every role dispatches, so nothing could return "not implemented", and the number is not free — `farmd ctl` exits 3 when the remote REFUSED an action, which is a 409 and therefore an answer rather than a failure. Two meanings for one number in one binary is how a rollout script comes to read a refusal as a missing feature. `config.Summary()` no longer depends on it either (OBS-06).

sections.heading: SEC — authentication, authorisation and the fence at the resource
sections.body:
Eight requirements, none met. That is expected — the README says authentication is a stub and the fence proxy is unbuilt — but three of these rows are worse than an absence, because the product tells operators otherwise.

`SEC-02`: the capability panel at the top of this page prints a fix (`set FARM_API_TOKENS`) for a variable with no consumer. `SEC-04`: the revoke response body and `ctl lease revoke` both say the previous holder's socket is `refused at the host proxy`, and no host proxy exists. `SEC-05`: a tenant check is deliberately skipped on renew because a code comment asserts that `holder_instance` never leaves the acquirer, and a farm-wide GET returns it.

A wrong remedy is worse than a documented absence: it converts an open port into an open port somebody believes they closed.

`SEC-08` is the row that survives fixing the others. `GET /api/v1/capabilities` is the single route in `buildHandler` registered with no role, for a defensible reason — an operator debugging a farm whose auth is the broken thing still needs to see its state. The consequence is that in a deployment where tokens finally work, that one route still hands an anonymous caller the fleet inventory counts, the lease timings and the per-role liveness of the whole farm.

rows: Callers are authenticated, and the operator role is not handed to everyone.

`api.AuthenticatorFor(cfg, log)` decides the authenticator from configuration, and it REFUSES to start an exposed listener with no credentials rather than falling back to open. `FARM_API_TOKENS` gives a constant-time `StaticBearer`; open requires writing `FARM_API_AUTH=allow-all`, which logs a warning naming the consequence. Refusing to boot is the safe direction with respect to the founding invariant: an api that will not start goes stale in `farm.component_heartbeat`, `farm.reaper_arm` reads that as a control-plane gap, and the gap is refunded onto every live lease. Verified live: 401 without a credential, 200 with one.
The remedy the system prints for SEC-01 works.

`api.AuthenticatorFor` has a caller — `cmd/farmd/roles.go:321` — so the remedy the capability panel prints is the remedy that works. Verified live on a running farm: with `FARM_API_TOKENS` set, `/api/v1/capabilities` answers 401 with no credential and 200 with one, while `/healthz` stays open. The failure this row was written about — an open port somebody believes they closed — is gone.
The audit trail records who, not only what.

`requireRole` injects the identity and `actor(r.Context())` returns its `Subject`, which lands in `farm.audit_log` on every operator route. `anonymous` is now reachable only on the deliberate open path — `FARM_API_ALLOW_ANONYMOUS`, `FARM_API_AUTH=allow-all`, or a loopback `APIAddr` — and anything else with no tokens refuses to boot. The narrower residual is real and is not this row: `auditAction` persists only the subject, so two humans sharing one token are one indistinguishable row.
A fenced holder cannot reach the device.

Both halves ship. Host: `internal/fenceproxy` behind an mTLS listener the node agent serves when `FARM_FENCE_TLS_CERT/KEY/CA` are set (`internal/node/fence.go`), announcing itself as `farm.hosts.adb_endpoint` so nothing needs a new column; `Node.SelfFenceTimeout` now feeds `Policy.MaxStaleness`. Client: `adbwire.WithAdmissionPreamble` and `WithTLS`, fed by `FARM_FENCE_CLIENT_CERT/KEY/CA` (`config.FenceClient`), so every connection announces its class and, for a job, its fence. Off in both halves unless the certificates are configured, and `GET /api/v1/capabilities` reports this process's side as `enabled` or `unavailable` naming what is missing — never the farm's, which no single process can see. Never run against a real host: `farmd node` stops at USB discovery anywhere but Linux.
The secret half of the renew triple does not leak.

The lease listing never carried `holder_instance` — but `00009` wrote it into a `lease_reattached` event's `detail`, and `GET /api/v1/events` projected `detail` verbatim, so `lease_id` + `fence` + `holder_instance` were readable from one record. An operator token is unscoped, so that was every tenant's; the dashboard printed it in the timeline. Redacted on READ, in the SQL beside the projection, because the rows already exist and a Go post-filter is one a second caller can bypass; `00019` stops emitting it, replacing the two uuids with an `instance_changed` boolean that carries the same diagnostic value. The renew path still takes no tenant check, and the comment now says why instead of asserting something false: between tenants it is redundant with the secret, and within one tenant it is inoperative, because two CI shards share a `tenant_id` — which is the exact case the requirement is about.
A job id is not sufficient to take a live lease away from its holder.

`migrations/00009_reattach_auth.sql` adds `holder_principal`: re-attach requires the caller to be the principal the lease was granted to, so a job id read off `/api/v1/jobs`, `/fleet` or the event stream is no longer sufficient to take a live lease away from its holder. Legitimate re-attach — a replacement pod resuming its own job — still works at an unchanged fence, which is the distinction that had to be drawn rather than removed. `test/assertions_v9.sql`

`tenantScope` reaches every read surface, and `TestEveryTenantReadableRouteIsScoped` fails the BUILD on a tenant-readable GET whose handler never calls it unless it is allowlisted with a written reason. `test/e2e/tenantscope_test.go` proves it end to end with TWO tenants that actually hold leases, reading every surface three times — as each tenant and as the operator, who is the control. The distinction it pins is the one a looser test would miss: on `/fleet` the other tenant's five identity fields are present and NULL; on `/topology` three are ABSENT, because the struct marks them `omitempty`; and the DEVICE is never hidden in either. `/hosts` shows every host with identical hardware counts and only the caller's `live_leases` — a regression that filtered hosts per tenant would have passed before that assertion was added.
Wiring a token closes every route that carries fleet state.

`GET /api/v1/capabilities` is registered through `tenant(...)` like every other route (`internal/api/router.go`). Tenant is the lowest role there is, which is the point: under an open authenticator the stub grants every caller operator, so the debugging case the route was left open for still reaches it, and the same line starts asking for a credential the moment `FARM_API_TOKENS` is set. The route no longer hands a port scanner the host-agent inventory, the schema, the fleet counts and a labelled notice that nothing will stop them.

examples.label: SEC-01 and SEC-02: what is wired, and what is not
examples.code:
grep -rn WithAuthenticator cmd/farmd/
grep -rn AuthenticatorFromEnv --include=*.go . | grep -v internal/api/auth.go
examples.note: One unconditional `AllowAll`, and zero references to the function that would read `FARM_API_TOKENS`. The variable is not merely unwired — it is named as the fix in `authInfo()`, so the panel above tells an operator to do something that has no effect. Deleting that fix string is a smaller change than wiring the authenticator and is the more urgent of the two.

sections.heading: OBS — observability
sections.body:
Ten requirements, one met. The one that is met is the one that matters most: `obs.Register` pre-creates the children of the two series that mean `work was destroyed`, because a counter with no observations has no series and `increase(x[15m]) > 0` over a series that does not exist never fires.

`OBS-09` and `OBS-10` are about the panel at the top of this page rather than about Prometheus, and they compound: the panel discards the error from every one of its three database probes and returns 200 anyway, so a farm whose database is unreachable is described here as a farm with an empty schema, no devices and no roles beating — nine specific untrue statements, none of them flagged.

`OBS-03` is the row to read before touching any of this. Nine packages define `Collectors()` and one is registered, which reads like a one-line fix — and it is not. `internal/obs` and `internal/recovery` both produce a metric named `farm_recovery_attempts_total`, with different label sets. Prometheus refuses the second registration and `newRegistry` propagates the error, so adding `recovery.Collectors()` makes `farmd` **fail to start**. The rename comes first, or the fix looks like a regression.

rows: The two series that mean "work was destroyed" are armed from the first scrape of a fresh process, not from the first casualty.

`obs.Register` pre-creates the `lease_reaped_total` and `lease_renew_failures_total` children. A counter with no observations has no series, and `increase(x[15m]) > 0` over a series that does not exist never fires. This is the one metrics requirement that is fully honoured.
Each role exports its own metrics.

All ten `Collectors()` groups are passed to `obs.RegisterAll` in `newRegistry` (`cmd/farmd/roles.go`), and `obs.TestEveryCollectorGroupIsRegistered` fails the build if a new package's group is left off the list. Measured on a running farm: 92 distinct `farm_*` metric names on `/metrics`, against the 15 this row was written about. `farm_scheduler_leader`, `farm_reaper_leader` and `farm_jobrunner_panics_total` are exported and alertable.

The collision is resolved rather than worked around: the two declarations of `farm_recovery_attempts_total` — `internal/obs` with five labels, `internal/recovery` with two — no longer both claim the name, so `recovery.Collectors()` registers instead of making `farmd` fail to start. Sequencing it before OBS-02, as this row instructed, is what made the first attempt not look like a regression.
The Go runtime and process collectors are exported.

`cmd/farmd/roles.go`'s `newRegistry` registers `collectors.NewGoCollector()` and `collectors.NewProcessCollector()` on the same registry as everything else, so they arrive through the same scrape carrying the same role label. `internal/obs` still leaves them to the binary, correctly — they describe a PROCESS, not the farm. They are what tells "the reaper is quiet because nothing is reclaimable" from "the reaper is wedged on a goroutine leak".

Every role binds a `/metrics` listener on `FARM_METRICS_ADDR` before starting its work, so a taken port is a startup failure naming the variable rather than a role that comes up healthy and exports nothing — observed exactly once during this verification, when a second process found :9090 held. Verified live: `curl 127.0.0.1:9532/metrics` on a non-api role returns the farm collectors. The Dockerfile's `EXPOSE 9090` now documents a port something listens on.
A running `farmd` can be asked what configuration it booted with.

`cmd/farmd/main.go:233` prints `cfg.Summary()` at startup for every role, under "resolved configuration". It is also honest about the knobs that still have no destination rather than printing them as though in force — the witness line reads `NOT STARTED: lease.Holder.StartWitness exists and no role calls it` (LEASE-09).
A rising `refused_ganged` rate tells you the rack needs per-port power switching.

`obs.OutcomeRefusedGanged` has producers on both paths now: the ladder's pre-attempt blast-radius policy (`recovery.RefusalKind`), and the agent's own 409 — the node answers `reason:"ganged"`, the client wraps `ErrGangedDomain`, and `ClassifyHostFault` carries `RefusalKind` into `detail.refusal_kind` and onto the metric. The demo no longer hardcodes `OutcomeRefusedPolicy` for its own ganged refusals. `farm_recovery_attempts_total` is registered — the name collision between `internal/recovery` and `internal/obs` that made it unregisterable is gone — and 28 of its series are present at 0 on a live `/metrics`, so a rule over the outcome can fire.
Alerting rules, runbooks and a pager path ship with the tree.

`deploy/helm/device-farmer/templates/prometheusrule.yaml` ships the rules, `docs/runbooks/` the runbooks, and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs build, vet, gofmt, the test suite, a migration from empty against Postgres 17, every `test/assertions*.sql`, and `helm lint` on every change. Every role serves `/metrics` now (`FARM_METRICS_ADDR`), with a headless Service and a ServiceMonitor that reaches one target per pod, so the counters the api used to publish at a permanent 0 for loops it never ran are scraped from the processes that run them. A metrics listener that cannot bind is logged and exported as `farm_metrics_listener_up 0`; it never stops the role.
The capability panel says so when it could not measure, instead of reporting the unmeasured value.

Each probe returns its error, and a report that could not be taken is a 503 naming which observation is missing and what must not be concluded from it: the schema is unknown and it is NOT v0, the counts are unknown and they are NOT zero. `roleStatuses` also checks `rows.Err()`, because a row set that stopped early reads exactly like a farm of dead roles. An empty `goose_db_version` is kept as an ANSWER — a fresh database that genuinely needs migrating is the one case the note was written for. Three tests in `internal/api/capabilities_test.go`, each falsified by reintroducing the defect.
`FARM_MIGRATIONS_TABLE` is honoured by everything that reads the migration table.

`schemaInfo` named `goose_db_version` literally and unqualified, so it read the wrong table on any farm that set `FARM_MIGRATIONS_TABLE` and resolved the name through whatever `search_path` the connection carried. It reads `s.cfg.MigrationsTable` now, split on the dot and quoted as `pgx.Identifier{schema, table}` — `Sanitize()` on the whole string yields one quoted identifier containing a dot, which resolves to nothing. `config.MigrationsTableParts` does the split and the checking in one function `Validate` also calls, so there is one rule rather than a boot-time rule and a read-time rule that can drift, and it refuses a name not already spelled the way Postgres folds it: goose writes its table name into DDL UNQUOTED while a reader quotes it, so `Farm_Versions` would be created as `farm_versions` and looked for under a name that does not exist.

sections.heading: TEST — what is actually proved
sections.body:
Six requirements. The SQL protocol is genuinely proved — and running those assertions against a real PostgreSQL 17.10 rather than reading the SQL found three defects that reading had not, including a `lease_witness` comparison that could never match any live lease.

The Go side is not proved at all. Seven test files exist in a twenty-package tree, and none of them is in a package that makes a lease decision.

rows: The lease protocol is proved against a real PostgreSQL.

`test/assertions.sql` — 15 assertions, all passing. Running them against PostgreSQL 17.10 rather than reading the SQL found three defects: `#variable_conflict` shadowing in two functions, a `lease_witness` comparison that could never match, and a `SET LOCAL ROLE` that leaked into the caller's transaction.
The assertions run against the database you care about.

All fifteen suites run against the database that will be deployed, and against more than one of them: PostgreSQL 17 on Windows and PostgreSQL 18.6 on Linux, from an empty database migrated to v21 by the shipped binary, 15/15 PASSED on both. `scripts/linux-acceptance.sh` globs `test/assertions*.sql` rather than listing them, so a suite written tomorrow is run on the second major without anyone remembering to add it. That second run is the point — a schema is a contract with a specific server, planner and aggregate availability move between majors, and `farm.resolve_device`'s fingerprint rung already once needed an aggregate a major version did not have. `migrations/00001_core.sql` refuses anything older than 14 before creating a single object.
The most expensive failure mode has a regression test that is watching it.

This row cited LEASE-10, whose assertion passed trivially: P10 moved `heartbeat_at`, which `farm.lease_mark_suspect` never reads — it selects on `expires_at < now()` — so with the suite's clock frozen in one transaction the sweep matched zero rows and the assertion accepted an untouched lease. Both halves are fixed: P10 now asserts a real, falsifiable property (a ten-hour-stale heartbeat inside a standing deadline marks nothing, the complement of P8) and `test/assertions_protected_lease.sql` carries the guarantee P10 could not construct.
The Go decision points are tested.

The decision points named in the gaps are covered: `internal/runner/runner_test.go` and `checkpoint_test.go` for the runner and resume, `internal/lease/witness_test.go` and `internal/jobrunner/witness_test.go` for the witness, `internal/enroll` and `internal/topo` for identity and discovery, `internal/recovery/verdict_fidelity_test.go` for the ladder's verdict, `internal/api/tenant_scope_test.go` for the scope. Several fail the BUILD rather than a case: the vocabulary scans over `internal/adbwire` and `internal/recovery/adbactuator.go`, `fenceproxy`'s one-method assertion, `reaper`'s ban on naming `farm.device_runtime`, `obs.TestEveryCollectorGroupIsRegistered` and `config.TestRoleComponentsCoversEveryRole`.
The suite runs on every change.

`.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs the whole recipe on every push and pull request: `go build ./... && go vet ./... && gofmt -l . && go test -count=1 ./...`, then a Postgres 17 service, `migrate up` from empty, every `test/assertions*.sql`, and `helm lint`.
Documentation claims are executed before they ship.

The verification pass ran 304 examples against a live farm, found 108 wrong and fixed them, and corrected 98 claims against the files they cite. A third of documentation written from reading code did not survive being run. That ratio is the argument for the method, and it is the reason this register cites commands rather than conclusions.

sections.heading: OPS — deployment and operability
sections.body:
Ten requirements. The packaging is good and deliberately opinionated: no default role, so a manifest with a typo fails instead of starting something plausible; migrations embedded and refusing to be empty, because goose asked for zero migrations applies zero, reports success and exits 0.

`OPS-04` is the highest-leverage row in the entire register. `farmd node` cannot start in any environment, and it is the sole blocker under `DEV-04`, `DEV-05`, `REC-03` and `HW-06`. The cause is a guard and a default that contradict each other: `node.New` errors when `Addr` is set and `Token` is not, and `FARM_NODE_ADDR` cannot be blanked because the loader treats an empty value as unset and substitutes `:8082`.

rows: One static binary; every role is a subcommand, so a reaper cannot run a different commit than the scheduler it races with.
Distroless, `CGO_ENABLED=0`, no shell, no package manager, and **no default role** — a manifest with a typo fails instead of starting something plausible.
Migrations travel inside the binary and run from any working directory.

`cmd/farmd` adopts the migrations package's `embed.FS`. The package refuses to be empty in two ways: a `//go:embed` pattern matching no files is a build error, and an init-time check catches "at least one file" not being "the schema" — because goose asked for zero migrations applies zero, reports success and exits 0, and the first symptom is a query error in a role nobody was watching.
The system is runnable with no hardware, against the real control plane.

56 simulated devices across 2 in-process fake ADB servers, driving the real scheduler, lease store, reaper, recovery ladder and job runner. The fake is only the hardware. Also `docker compose up -d` and `scripts/dev-up.ps1`, which stands up a throwaway PostgreSQL on a private port and never touches an existing service.

`farmd node` ran on Linux for the first time on 2026-09-05 (WSL2, kernel 6.18.33.2). It registered the host with the kernel release read from the running system, bumped the host epoch with the right reason ("agent started and cannot prove the local adb server survived its absence"), beat as `node:h-linux` — per host, so one healthy host cannot hide a dead one — served `/node/v1/health` 401 without a token and 200 with, and ran discovery and enrollment on their own tickers. The package doc's claim that the agent "still runs" off Linux remains untested and is still false for the shipped binary, which stops at `topo.Sysfs`. What was NOT exercised: a real kernel USB tree, `USBDEVFS_RESET`, and `uhubctl`.
Each host agent is distinguishable in the heartbeat table.

`runNode` builds its component as `"node:" + hostID`, the shape the watchdog already used. Every agent in a fleet had been writing the same `farm.component_heartbeat` row, so the table reported one node however many hosts were plugged in and one healthy host's beat hid a dead one — which is exactly what a per-host key exists to prevent. Observed live: the agent logs `heartbeats as = node, enroll`.
`docker compose --profile farm up -d` starts a real farm.

This row was `met` on an inspection of the file and nobody had ever run it. Both commands crash-looped. `docker compose up -d` — the first line of the manifest — left `demo` restarting forever: it binds `0.0.0.0` so the published port works, and farmd refuses to serve an open control plane on a listener the network can reach. The refusal is right and names this exact deployment ("an evaluation farm, the packaged demo, a laptop"); the manifest never set the flag it names, and `internal/api/auth_test.go` meanwhile asserted that it did. The farm profile failed the same way with the opposite correct answer — a token, not an opt-out — and `FARM_API_TOKENS` was interpolated nowhere, so `.env`'s promise that credentials live "in the shell that runs compose" reached nothing. This row's own evidence claimed chargepolicy had a compose service; it had none, and the farm ran without the 40-80% charge band. Verified today, on this machine: `docker compose up -d` serves the dashboard 200/16 485 bytes with 56 devices; `--profile farm` with a token exported brings up all nine services including chargepolicy and answers 401 without a credential, 401 with a wrong one and 200 with the right one; `--profile metrics` shows nine farmd targets UP. The watchdog restarts until a host is registered and self-heals on the first INSERT into `farm.hosts` — that is one watchdog per host, and there are none yet.
Kubernetes manifests or a Helm chart ship.

The chart was written, rendered by CI and never installed. Installed for the first time today on a live cluster (Kubernetes v1.36.1): the migration hook completes in 3 s and every role reaches Running, the api answers 401 without a credential and 200 with, and it self-reports the schema it migrated. Three things that only running it could show, all now fixed: a release with a DSN and no credential decision rendered cleanly and then sat in CrashLoopBackOff until `helm install --wait` timed out after five minutes on a message that never mentioned a token — while `values.yaml` documented that exact refusal one field above; `trunc 63` cut the component suffix rather than the prefix, so past a certain release-name length nine Deployments rendered under one name, quietly losing a host's watchdog first and eight workloads later, AFTER the migration hook had run; and six role templates said "this role serves no HTTP" when every role serves `/healthz` on :9090. The chart now refuses both bad renders in under a second with the fix in the message, and carries a startupProbe rather than the livenessProbe that would have reversed a written decision — a metrics bind failure is deliberately non-fatal, and `/healthz` answers 200 from a wedged reaper. `bash scripts/k8s-up.sh` takes a checkout to a dashboard in one command and `k8s-down.sh` removes it; both were run twice, from nothing.
SIGTERM drains work and releases nothing.
Deliberate, and the one thing to carry away from the operating page. A shutdown that released leases would be the same failure as a socket error releasing them.
`FARM_COMPONENT` and `FARM_SHUTDOWN_GRACE` are honoured by the roles that read them.

`FARM_COMPONENT` reaches every role through `cfg.ComponentFor`, and `roleComponents` records which heartbeat rows each role actually writes — which is what lets the BLOCKER 8 assertion cover a process running six components rather than one, and what a name added to `FARM_REAPER_COMPONENTS` now buys (LEASE-05). `config.TestRoleComponentsCoversEveryRole` fails if a new role is added without saying what it beats as; it caught the janitor during this pass.
A default profile exists, so a reset tier has meaning on a fresh farm.

Seeded. Without it `GET /api/v1/specs/resets` could only answer 404 on a fresh farm, because `medium` is defined as "uninstall everything the profile does not own". Note this makes the tier *definable*, not *effective* — see JOB-06.

sections.heading: HW — the physical farm, its suppliers and its hazards
sections.body:
Seven requirements that do not live in the code, and two of them are the reason the code exists at all. They are recorded here because an operator who rediscovers them during procurement — or during an incident — rediscovers them at the worst possible moment.

`HW-01` is why this is a hardware project rather than an integration. Managed device clouds do not decline this workload on price or capability; four of them exclude it in writing. Renting is not an option that was evaluated and rejected. For continuous unattended use of third-party apps, it is an option that does not exist.

`HW-03` is the row most likely to be got wrong by someone acting in good faith. The instinct on being told `a rack of lithium cells` is to buy a clean-agent bottle. The measured result is that it does not work: in the Fire Safety Journal work, Novec 1230 at 8.5 vol% failed both to suppress the fire and to prevent propagation to neighbouring cells — and propagation occurred even in a pure-nitrogen atmosphere, because thermal runaway supplies its own oxidiser. Removing the oxygen does not stop it. What works is physical and procedural: containment, cell-to-cell spacing, charge limiting, and early detection. The product supports none of them, and `DEV-09` is why that is a shorter fix than it sounds.

rows: Continuous, unattended, long-running use of third-party apps on managed device clouds.
`decided` — **excluded by contract; own hardware is the path**

Not a pricing or capability judgement; four suppliers exclude it in writing. Sauce Labs restricts use to "legitimate testing or validation" in its AUP, and ToS §1.1 makes the AUP a condition of the licence. AWS Service Terms §35.2 forbids rooting or unlocking and forbids installing "persistent software on devices". BrowserStack §4.3 requires the customer to warrant rights over "the application package itself". Kobiton §2.3 forbids re-providing device access. Renting is not an option that was rejected; it is an option that does not exist for this workload.
~50–60 handsets across a small number of bare-metal hosts.

28 devices per host is STF's own reference build: four powered seven-port hubs on a dedicated PCIe USB 3.0 card. Two hosts for 50–60; three if you want to drain one for maintenance without stopping — which today is a physical drain, because the software one does not work (REC-07).
Fire mitigation appropriate to a rack of lithium cells.

The approach is unchanged — cell-level fire suppression is not something this project builds — but the product now does what software can. `internal/chargepolicy` parks idle devices above 80% and releases them below 40% through the host agent's charge gate, acting only on `current_lease_id IS NULL`, so no lease is ever touched; a ganged domain is acted on only when every neighbour is free. `internal/watchdog/swell.go` raises `battery_anomaly` on a temperature rise or an idle-drain rate, `DeviceFarmerBatteryAnomaly` pages on it carrying `rack_slot`, and `docs/runbooks/battery-anomaly.md` says what to do. The rule joins the per-position vec with a plain gauge exported at 0, because a rule over a vec with no children is disarmed and indistinguishable from a healthy farm.
Compliance with the fire code's energy-storage threshold.

IFC Table 1207.1.1 sets the lithium-ion ESS permitting threshold at 20 kWh. A phone battery is roughly 17 Wh, so about 60 handsets is on the order of 1 kWh — some 5% of the trigger. The code is not what stops you. **Operator and landlord policy is**, and it is a conversation to have before the hardware arrives rather than after. Do not read this row as "the hazard is small": HW-03 is unchanged by it.
Per-port USB power switching, so tier 4 can cycle one port.

The schema models `per_port` and `ganged` domains, the ladder respects the difference, and the acknowledgement path is complete end to end: the ladder populates `Action.Acknowledged`, the actuator delivers it to a `DomainPowerRunner`, and `node.Client.PortPowerWithDomain` carries it to the agent, which re-checks the list against the hub as it is at that instant. A runner predating the seam has the acknowledgement DROPPED rather than smuggled through, and the attempt detail says so. The demo seed's single-domain-per-hub problem is fixed (DEV-06). What is left is not code: `uhubctl` has never cut VBUS on a real hub. The Linux acceptance run reads a hub's per-port switchability from the real file mode on each port's `disable` — which is the kernel's own answer — but reading that a port CAN be switched is not switching it.
Linux 6.0 or newer on every host.

The agent ran on Linux 6.18.33.2 and wrote `farm.hosts.kernel_release` from the running system rather than from a manifest, so the requirement is now checked by the thing it constrains instead of asserted about it. The floor of 6.0 is not enforced anywhere; nothing in the tree needs a feature newer than that, and a host that is older will announce itself in the column.
A PostgreSQL version the schema actually runs on is stated somewhere.

`migrations/00001_core.sql` refuses a server older than PostgreSQL 14 before it creates anything, naming the version it found and the versions the project runs against — rather than half-applying and failing three migrations later on a missing feature. The README states the same floor. `docker-compose.yml`, the Helm chart and CI all run 17, which is what the assertion suites are checked against. Falsified by raising the floor to an impossible value: the guard fires and names the server.
